title: Practice: scatter graphs and correlation
intro: Nine questions on describing and using correlation.

questions.prompt: Match each pair of variables to the correlation you would expect.

left.text: Height above sea level and boiling point of water
A person's mass and their history test score
Size of car and fuel economy (km per litre)

hints: Ask: as the first goes up, what happens to the second?
questions.explanation: Taller people have longer arms (positive). Water boils at a lower temperature higher up (negative). Mass has nothing to do with history scores (none). Bigger cars go fewer km per litre (negative).

questions.prompt: Time taken to write a name backwards against its number of letters. Click the **outlier**.
hints: Look for the point furthest from the general upward trend.
questions.explanation: The point $(6, 3.3)$ — Hannah — sits well below the trend. Her name is a palindrome, which is why it was so quick.

questions.prompt: Select **every** true statement about lines of best fit.

options.text: It should follow the trend of the points
It must pass through the origin
There should be roughly as many points above it as below
You should draw one even when there is no correlation
It can be used to estimate one variable from the other

hints: A line of best fit only makes sense when there is a trend.
questions.explanation: It follows the trend with points balanced either side and lets you estimate. It does not have to go through the origin, and with no correlation you should not draw one.

questions.prompt: A line of best fit for age against yearly earnings passes through $(25, 22\,000)$ and $(57, 36\,000)$. Estimate the earnings of a 48-year-old, to the nearest thousand dollars.
hints: The gradient is $14\,000 \div 32 = 437.5$ dollars per year.

questions.prompt: Using the same line, estimate the age of someone earning 23 000 dollars a year.
hints: $23\,000$ is $1000$ more than $22\,000$. How many years is that at $437.5$ per year?

questions.prompt: Height above sea level (m) and boiling point (°C): (1000, 96), (1600, 94), (2200, 92), (3600, 88), (4800, 84), (6400, 78), (7200, 76). Estimate the boiling point at 3000 m.
hints: 3000 m lies between 2200 m (92 °C) and 3600 m (88 °C).
questions.explanation: Between 92 °C and 88 °C, a little over halfway — about 90 °C. The data shows strong negative correlation.

questions.prompt: Book pages against mass (g). Which point is the heaviest book? Click it.
hints: The heaviest book is the highest point.
questions.explanation: The highest point is $(180, 360)$ — the book with the most pages is also the heaviest, which fits the strong positive correlation.

questions.prompt: If two variables show a strong positive correlation, an increase in one must **cause** an increase in the other.
hints: Think of ice-cream sales and sunburn.
questions.explanation: False. Correlation shows a link, not a cause. Both could be caused by something else (such as hot weather), or it could be coincidence.

questions.prompt: Habibah plots arm length against hours of TV for five friends and sees a positive correlation. What is the best response?

options.text: Five people is too small a sample, and there is no sensible link — it is probably coincidence
Longer arms make people watch more TV
Watching TV makes your arms grow
The graph must have been drawn wrongly

hints: How much can you conclude from five people?
questions.explanation: A tiny sample can easily show a pattern by chance, and there is no plausible reason for a link. The graph may be correct — the conclusion is what is wrong.
